classification.difficultyReason: Calculate exclusive and neither region counts from overlapping totals, then use these counts to find probabilities.

content.prompt: A survey of 50 families showed that 28 owned a cat, 30 owned a dog and 15 owned both a dog and a cat.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Represent this information on a Venn diagram.

answer.short: Let $C$ represent families owning a cat and $D$ represent families owning a dog. Cat only: 13; both: 15; dog only: 15; neither: 7.
answer.worked:
Let $C$ represent families owning a cat and $D$ represent families owning a dog. Place 15 in the overlap.

$$\begin{aligned}\text{Cat only}&=28-15=13\\\text{Dog only}&=30-15=15\\\text{Neither}&=50-(13+15+15)=7\end{aligned}$$

spec.description: Unshaded two-set Venn diagram inside the sample-space rectangle. C denotes cat ownership and D denotes dog ownership.
spec.mathematics: C only contains 13 families, the intersection contains 15, D only contains 15, and neither contains 7; total 50.
spec.answerVisibility: Complete solution figure; absent from the student prompt.

children.label: b
children.prompt: One family is selected at random from the group. What is the probability that the family owns:

children.label: i
children.prompt: a cat but not a dog?

answer.worked:
There are $28-15=13$ families that own a cat but not a dog.

$$P(\text{cat but not dog})=\frac{13}{50}.$$

children.label: ii
children.prompt: a dog but not a cat?

answer.worked:
There are $30-15=15$ families that own a dog but not a cat.

$$P(\text{dog but not cat})=\frac{15}{50}=\frac{3}{10}.$$

children.label: iii
children.prompt: neither a dog nor a cat?

answer.worked:
There are $13+15+15=43$ families owning at least one of the two animals, so $50-43=7$ own neither.

$$P(\text{neither dog nor cat})=\frac{7}{50}.$$
